# The Things We Keep Running

On the hottest day of the summer, the sign outside the repair shop fell off the wall.

It had been hanging by one screw for months. The heat softened something—the paint, perhaps, or the old wood behind it—and by noon the sign was lying faceup on the pavement. **BELL & DAUGHTER: REPAIRS**, it said, though there had never been a Bell in the shop during any of the years I knew it. Beneath the name, in smaller letters, someone had once promised radios, lamps, small appliances, and clocks. A previous owner had crossed out *clocks* with a strip of black paint. You could still read it if you looked closely.

I was passing on my way to the hardware store when I saw Mara trying to lift the sign. It was heavier than it looked. We carried it inside together, each of us holding one end, and set it against a cabinet full of parts. The shop smelled of warm dust and metal. On the counter lay a fan with its grille removed, its blades motionless.

“Can you fix that?” I asked.

“Probably.”

I had meant the sign.

Mara followed my glance. “That too, probably. Different problem.”

I offered to hold it while she put in a new screw, but she said the wall needed work first. The wood was rotten around the hole. A bigger screw would hold for a while, then pull out a larger piece. She had a way of saying such things without making them sound like lessons, which meant I often noticed the lesson anyway.

I bought my lightbulbs and came back the next morning with a cassette recorder.

It had belonged to my mother. For years it had lived in the back of a closet, under a shoe box full of extension cords. When I found it, I remembered her pressing its red button to record messages for relatives overseas. She would begin formally, asking after everyone’s health, and then get distracted by ordinary details: a stubborn stain on the kitchen ceiling, a neighbor’s new dog, the price of peaches. She talked until the tape clicked off.

After she died, I kept the recorder but never tried it. Its plastic case was scratched, and one corner was held together with cloudy tape. I could have bought a working cassette player online. What I wanted, though, was to put the little machine she had held on a table and hear it play.

Mara made no promise. She opened the battery compartment, tilted it toward the light, and showed me the blue-green crust on the contacts.

“We can clean that,” she said. “Leave it here.”

The shop had been on Alder Street longer than I had lived in the city. Between a pharmacy and a store that sold phone cases, its narrow window displayed a rotating selection of things waiting for their owners: a desk lamp with a green shade, a kitchen scale, an electric train engine no longer than my hand. Mara wrote each customer’s name on a paper tag and tied it to the cord or handle. If an object had no place to tie a tag, she used blue painter’s tape.

I started stopping in on my walks home from work. At first I told myself I was checking on the recorder. Mara was usually busy, and I learned to ask only when she looked up. I watched her replace a plug, test a toaster’s heating elements, and search a drawer for a spring that seemed too small to matter. People came in carrying their broken things with an expression I recognized: a little embarrassed by the object, and a little hopeful on its behalf.

One afternoon, a man brought in a coffee grinder. He set it on the counter and explained that his wife used it every morning. Then he explained that she had died in February.

Mara turned the grinder over to inspect the base. “Does it still make any noise?”

“A hum,” he said. “No grinding.”

“Leave it with me.”

When he had gone, I asked whether she could repair it.

“I’ll find out.”

“You said it as if you already knew.”

“He didn’t need to stand here while I took it apart.”

That was how she worked. Some things she could fix quickly, while their owners waited. Others took weeks because a part was hard to find or she wanted to ask someone about a model she hadn’t seen before. A few could not be repaired safely. She called the owners herself when that happened. I heard her do it once, and heard her offer to give the appliance back assembled, though it would never run. The person on the other end wanted it returned.

In late August, the power went out across our part of the city. A transformer had failed during the evening rush, leaving the traffic lights dark and the apartments without air-conditioning. People stood on sidewalks holding their phones up, looking for news. In the upper floors, windows opened one after another. Our building’s hallway, usually cool and empty, filled with footsteps.

I went outside because it was cooler there. Mara was sitting on a folding chair in front of the shop, working on a battery-powered lantern. Several neighbors had gathered around her. She tightened a contact, switched it on, and handed it to the woman who had brought it. The small white light drew everyone’s faces toward it.

“The heat got us,” somebody said.

“The equipment was old,” somebody else replied.

Both were true, as far as I could tell. We stayed outside until long after dark, trading rumors about when the power would return. Someone brought out water. A boy rolled a basketball gently from one side of the street to the other. Without the shop lights, I could barely see through Mara’s window, but I knew what was inside: the crowded shelves, the paper tags, the sign propped against the cabinet because the wall still hadn’t been repaired.

The electricity came back a little after midnight. One by one, the windows shut. By morning the street looked ordinary, except for a row of water bottles people had left beside the shop door.

A week later Mara called to say the recorder was working. When I arrived, she placed it on the counter beside a pair of small speakers.

“The motor belt had gone loose,” she said. “The contacts cleaned up well.”

She pressed *play* without a cassette in it so I could hear the mechanism turn. It made a dry, steady sound. Then she stopped it and asked whether I had a tape to try.

I did. I had brought one in my pocket, wrapped in a handkerchief. There was no label on the cassette. I remembered finding it years earlier in the same box as the recorder, but I had no idea what was on it.

Mara put it in. For a moment there was only hiss. Then my mother’s voice came out of the speakers, distant and unmistakable. She was asking someone whether they had received the photographs. She mentioned my uncle, a birthday dinner, and a recipe she had promised to send. In the background I could hear dishes being moved. I was trying to place the year when she broke off to ask, “Is that rain?”

There was a pause. A younger voice answered her. It was mine.

I had forgotten how impatient I sounded at fifteen. I told her it was only the sprinkler next door and asked if I could use the phone. She told me to wait until she finished. I made a noise of protest. Then, with perfect composure, she returned to her message and described the weather.

Mara stood at the far end of the counter, giving me room. I listened to the tape click and hiss and continue. My mother was alive in its few minutes only in the plain sense that she had been alive when she spoke. The tape held her voice, not her thoughts. I could not tell her I was sorry for the things I had said at fifteen, or ask whether she had received an answer about the photographs. I could hear her take a breath before beginning her next sentence. That was more than I had expected to have.

At home I listened to the whole cassette. One side contained the message; the other held part of a radio program, recorded over by accident. Halfway through the message, my mother said the microphone was too close to the window and moved it. The sound of traffic grew faint. She finished with a request for news from everyone, however small, and said goodbye twice.

For several days I carried the recorder from room to room. I played the tape while I cooked and once while I folded laundry. Eventually I put it on a shelf. I still wanted to hear her voice, but listening required a decision. I found that I preferred knowing I could make one.

In September, a notice appeared in Mara’s window. The building had been sold. The new owner intended to renovate, and her lease would not be renewed in the spring. Someone had written **SAVE BELL & DAUGHTER** on a piece of cardboard and taped it beneath the notice. People began bringing Mara addresses for empty storefronts and names of friends who might know someone with space. She thanked them, filed the scraps of paper in a folder, and went on working.

One Saturday I helped her sort a shelf at the back of the shop. There were cracked cases she had saved for their screws, manuals for appliances no one had brought in for years, and three shoeboxes of power adapters. She tested each adapter before deciding where it belonged. I thought we were getting ready for a move, but Mara said she sorted that shelf every autumn. She had found two screws she’d been looking for since June.

We stopped for lunch on the shop steps. I asked about the name on the sign.

“Mr. Bell started the place,” she said. “His daughter ran it after him. I bought it from her.”

“Why keep their name?”

“People knew where to come.”

She told me she had learned repair work in her father’s garage. He fixed bicycles and lawn mowers for neighbors, and she liked opening things to see why they had stopped. Later she took a course in electronics, worked for a company that serviced office equipment, and, when that job disappeared, came to Alder Street. Mr. Bell’s daughter had stayed for a month to show her where everything was.

I asked if she planned to put the sign up again. She looked at its empty place on the wall.

“After I move,” she said. “No point fixing that wall for the landlord.”

Through the winter, customers kept arriving. Some came because they had always come. Others had seen the notice and seemed newly anxious to use the shop while it was there. Mara worked her usual hours and searched for a place when she could. A location she liked cost too much. Another had enough room but no safe way to vent her soldering station. For a while she considered sharing a workspace across town, though it would have been difficult for many of her customers to reach.

By February she had found a narrow ground-floor unit near the library, twelve blocks away. The rent was manageable, and its front room had a window wide enough for the workbench. She signed the lease, then worried aloud about moving the shelves.

On moving day, I arrived to find six people already carrying boxes. The man with the coffee grinder had borrowed a van. The woman whose lantern Mara had repaired brought a hand truck. Two teenagers who lived above the pharmacy took turns wrapping the desk lamps in blankets. The grinder worked again; its owner mentioned this while directing the van toward the curb, as though I had asked. Mara handed out coffee and assigned tasks. By afternoon the old shop was empty except for dust outlines on the walls and the sign.

We carried it out last. The paint had worn off its lower edge, and one of the letters in **DAUGHTER** was almost gone. It still weighed as much as it had in August. At the new place, Mara set it against the wall while she decided where it should hang. Someone offered to fetch a drill. She ran her hand over the plaster, found a sturdy place beside the door, and asked him to make the holes.

I have moved apartments twice since then. The cassette recorder sits in the living room of the second one, near the books. Once a year or so, I play the tape. I listen all the way through, including the stretch where my younger self interrupts. I used to wish I could cut that part out. Now I’m glad nobody did. My mother’s small pause and my own sharp voice put us back in the kitchen together, with dishes on the counter and a sprinkler running next door.

The repair shop is a little farther from my usual route, but I still go in. Last month I took Mara a desk fan that had begun to rattle. She took off the grille and found a blade loose on its shaft. I waited while she secured it and checked the cord. When she switched the fan on, it pushed a gentle current of air across the counter and stirred the paper tags hanging there.

I paid her, picked up the fan, and walked home past the library. The day was warm, though nowhere near as hot as the day the sign fell. At the crossing I stopped for the light and felt the fan’s handle settle against my fingers. At home, I would set it by the window, plug it in, and let it run.
